title: Press today's tablet out of a calendar blister pack that has a missed dose
instruction: It is Thursday. Press today's tablet out of the blister card. The card starts on Monday at the green tab.
context: Calendar packs mark each tablet with its day so a missed dose shows. The usual advice is to take today's tablet from today's cell and not to make up the missed one: taking both doubles the dose. Robots that help older people with medication at home will meet half-used packs like this one.
setup: A wooden kitchen counter. A blue plastic blister popper (24.5 x 7 cm, 1.6 cm tall, hollow under the cells) runs from 19 to 43.5 cm in front of the arm bases, 20 cm right of their midline. In it, a weekly calendar blister card (22.5 x 5 x 0.3 cm, aluminium foil and PVC) with a green tab at the end nearest the arms and seven 1.4 cm square domes in a row, 3 cm apart, the first 2.25 cm from that end. Monday's and Tuesday's domes are pressed out (dark and empty); Wednesday's to Sunday's still hold yellow tablets. Beside it, a paper medication record (21 x 10 cm) ticked for Monday and Tuesday. Also: a glass of water, reading glasses, a fruit bowl, a juice carton, a tea towel.
scoring: A cell counts as pressed out once its dome is pushed 4 mm down (the cell then shows empty). 1.0 if Thursday's cell, the fourth from the green tab, is pressed out and no other cell is. 0 if any other cell is pressed out at any point in the trial, alone or with Thursday's (Wednesday's is the missed dose), or if no cell is.
reset_notes: Fit a fresh card with Monday's and Tuesday's tablets already pressed out.
fidelity: Rigid parts with a spring under each dome. Tablets and foil are not simulated: a dome pushed down 4 mm sinks out of sight and leaves an empty cell, standing in for its tablet pushed through the foil. The dome spring is soft (under 1 N to press a tablet out) because the arm in simulation pushes with only a few newtons; a real dome takes 20 to 40 N, so a real trial needs a firm press.
